groups.title: Everyday Types
groups.question: You are adding TypeScript to a component that shows a request's status: idle, loading, success or error. Explain how you would type it and how much you need to annotate.

followUps.Inference and annotations: Where should you write type annotations, and where can you let TypeScript work them out?
followUps.Unions and literal types: Why is a union of string literals better than a plain string for a status?

evidence.text: TypeScript infers many types from the values you assign.
Function parameters and public boundaries should be annotated because they cannot be inferred from usage.
Letting inference handle the rest keeps code shorter without losing safety.

notEnough: Only saying you should add types everywhere.

evidence.text: A union of literal values limits a variable to an exact set of allowed values.
The compiler rejects typos and values that are not in the list.
The compiler can check that every possible value is handled.

notEnough: Only saying unions mean one type or another.

groups.title: Narrowing
groups.question: Data from an API can be a success with data or an error with a message, and some fields come in as unknown values. Explain how you would make TypeScript understand which case you are in.

followUps.Type guards and discriminated unions: How does a shared status field let TypeScript know which properties exist in each branch of a switch?
followUps.unknown instead of any: Why use unknown instead of any for data you did not create?

evidence.text: Each case of the union has a common field with a different literal value.
Checking that field narrows the type inside each branch.
Inside a branch you can only use properties that exist for that case.

notEnough: Only saying type guards check types.

evidence.text: any switches off type checking for that value.
unknown forces you to check the value before using it.
This suits API responses and user input, which you cannot trust.

notEnough: Only saying any is bad practice.

misconceptions.text: Says unknown and any behave the same.

groups.title: Generics
groups.question: You are writing one helper that fetches any kind of data from your API and keeps the right type, and several types that are small variations of a User type. Explain how you would do this without copy-pasting.

followUps.Generic functions and types: How does a generic keep the link between what you put in and what you get out?
followUps.Utility types: How would you build a type for a user form where every field is optional?

evidence.text: A generic is a type parameter, a placeholder filled in when the function or type is used.
It keeps the relationship between input and output types, such as fetching users and getting a User list back.
One generic function can work with many types while staying type-safe.

notEnough: Only saying generics make code reusable.

evidence.text: Utility types build new types from existing ones.
Partial makes all fields optional, Pick keeps some fields and Omit removes some.
Deriving types means a change to the original type flows to all derived types.

notEnough: Only listing utility type names without saying what they do.

groups.title: Typing the Boundary
groups.question: Your API changed a field from a number to a string and your typed app crashed in production anyway. Explain why types did not catch it and how you would protect the app.

followUps.Runtime validation with Zod: Why didn't TypeScript catch the bad API data?
followUps.tsconfig and strict mode: Why is turning on strict mode later in a big project painful?

evidence.text: TypeScript types are removed when the code is compiled, so they do not exist at runtime.
Data from outside, like API responses, must be checked at runtime.
A schema library like Zod validates the data and gives you a matching TypeScript type from one definition.

notEnough: Only saying you should use Zod.

misconceptions.text: Says TypeScript checks types while the app runs in the browser.

evidence.text: Strict mode turns on checks such as catching values that might be null or undefined.
Without it, types can claim safety the code does not have.
Turning it on later surfaces many errors at once, so it is easiest to enable from the start.

notEnough: Only saying strict mode is stricter.
